questions.enonce_markdown:
Distinguish between the following:

(i) Economies of scale and diseconomies of scale. (4 marks)

(ii) Division of labour and efficiency of labour. (4 marks)

(iii) Specific and non-specific factors of production. (4 marks)

(12 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction.** In each pair the two terms are related, but they do not mean the same thing.

**(i) Economies of scale and diseconomies of scale (4 marks)**

| | Economies of scale | Diseconomies of scale |
|---|---|---|
| Meaning | The **fall in the average (unit) cost of production** as a firm **increases its output** (grows larger). | The **rise in the average (unit) cost** when a firm becomes **too large**. |
| Effect on cost | Cost per unit goes **down**. | Cost per unit goes **up**. |
| Causes | Bulk buying, use of machines, specialisation of labour, cheaper loans, spreading of advertising and administrative costs. | Management problems, delays in communication, poor co-ordination, workers' loss of interest and labour disputes. |
| Example | A big bakery in Douala buys flour in large quantities at a lower price per bag. | A firm with too many branches cannot supervise them, and waste increases. |

**(ii) Division of labour and efficiency of labour (4 marks)**

- **Division of labour** is the **splitting of the production of a good into several tasks**, each one performed by a different worker, so that every worker **specialises** in one task (for example, in a shirt factory one worker cuts, another sews, another irons).
- **Efficiency of labour** is the **productivity of workers**, that is the **amount of output a worker produces in a given time** (or the ability to produce more with the same effort and resources).
- *Difference:* division of labour is a **method of organising production**, while efficiency of labour is the **result** measured in output per worker. Division of labour is one of the causes of higher efficiency of labour, along with training, health and tools.

**(iii) Specific and non-specific factors of production (4 marks)**

- A **specific factor** can be used for **only one purpose** (or very few), so it is **not easily transferred** to another use. Examples: a cocoa-processing machine, a railway line, a trained brain surgeon.
- A **non-specific (mobile) factor** can be **used for many different purposes** and moved easily between uses. Examples: a plot of land that can grow maize or be used for housing, unskilled labour, a pick-up truck, money capital.
- *Importance:* specific factors have **low occupational mobility** and may be unemployed if demand for their product falls, whereas non-specific factors adapt easily.

questions.enonce_markdown:
Explain four determinants of efficiency of labour.

(8 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction.** The **efficiency (productivity) of labour** is the output a worker produces per unit of time. It depends on the following determinants.

**1. Education and training.** Workers who have gone to school and received technical training or on-the-job training understand their tasks, make fewer mistakes and use machines properly. For example, a trained mechanic repairs more vehicles in a day than an untrained one.

**2. Health and nutrition.** Healthy, well-fed workers are strong, work longer hours, miss fewer days through illness and concentrate better. Diseases such as malaria reduce the number of working days and lower output.

**3. Wages, incentives and working conditions.** Good pay, bonuses, promotion prospects, job security, safe workplaces and good relations with employers **motivate** workers to give their best. Poor pay and bad conditions lead to absenteeism and low effort.

**4. Capital equipment and technology.** Workers who have **modern tools and machines** produce more than those working by hand. A farmer with a tractor cultivates more land per day than one using a hoe.

**Other determinants** include the **division of labour** (specialisation increases skill and speed), the quality of management and organisation, and the climate and attitude to work.

**Conclusion.** Better education, health, motivation and equipment raise labour efficiency, and this raises output and incomes.
